It is now something more than ten years since the tory administration of the Duke of Wellington and Sir K. feel was drawing to a close. We heard of no public meetings then to pass resolutions in its lavour þÿ of no requisitions from the first cities of the kingdom, to invite its leading members to become candi. dates. Instead of going into the city to attend a crowded meeting of electors, with the first bankers and commercial men in London at their head, Sir Robert Reel's last act was, if ,ve recollect right, to advise the king to decline an invitation to dine with the lord maver, because the unpopularity of his ministers was so great that it was feared that their presence might occasion a popular tumult. The following extract from the Annual Register, for the year 1830, gives a picture of the state in which the lories handed over the country to the liberal party, after an almost uninterrupted possession of power lor fifty years. " Night after night, new conflagrations were lighted up by bands of incendiaries : cornslacks, barns, farm buildings, and live stock were consumed indiscriminately. Bolder bands attacked mills and demolished machinery. All protection for properly seemed to be at an end Bands of rioters pillaged and destroyed during the day, and, so soon as night fell, simultaneous conflagrations, starting up in different quarters, spread over the country horror and dismay. The military force in the disturbed counties was increased ; a pro-

clamation was issued offering a reward of £500 for the conviction of any person engaged in fire-raisings ; and a special commission was ordered to proceed into the shires where the outrages were committed." Such is a picture from the pen of a contemporary writer of the concluding scene of the fifty years' tory þÿreign such the net result w hich they had to show for 1500 millions of the nation's money, squandered in a useless war þÿ to such a pass had the system of ' coercing the unruly wiils of the people," bv Man- Chester massacres, brought the affairs of the nation. There is a good homely adage, that the " proof of the pudding is in the eating." Was the country belter or worse off", was it more or less tranquil at home, more or less respected abroad ; did it, in short, preseut more or (ewer signs of a well governed country fen years ago, after fifty years of tory government, than it does now, after ten years of liberal govei n/nent ? This is a plain question, which any one can answer for himself. The contrast between the present condition of the country and its condition when the tones quitted office, is not greater than that between the professions and principles of the two governments. The last tory government of which Sir Robert l'eel was a prominent member, gave the country the present cornlaws, and refused even such a scanty measure of reform as the transfer of a single representative from East Retford to Birmingham. þÿ Mr Huskisson, whose name was identified

with the cause of commercial reform, was tuined out of the cabinet because his views were too liberal. The opportunity afforded bv a large surplus revenue was allowed to pass without any attempt to repeal the duties on coals, candles, soap, and other articles of general consumption, which pressed most heavily on the labouring classes In lact,

Tasimraasx atatttmawBs A.TI3» the whole policy of the Reel-Wellington administration, during the last years of its existence, seemed to be directed towards the single end of patching up the old league between torvism. monopoly, and intolerance, which had been shaken by the one liberal measure of catholic emancipation loiced upon the government by its fears. How different is the situation of the present government. On the eve of an appeal to the nation, it can say boldly, " Look for yourselves, whether we have neglected the interests of the country or mismanaged its resources ; whether we have governed it better or worse than the men v ho preceded us. Examine, for we court inquiry, whether there is any spot on the habitable globe on which you can lav your linger, and say þÿ here the interests or honour of England have suffered under a liberal administration. Go to our colonies ; Go to Canada, to Australia, or India, and ask whether the government of your colonial empire has been better conducted by us or by our tory predecessors. Go to Ireland, and inquire what military force is sufficient now to insure tranquility, and what was sufficient under ihe tory regime ; how many cases ol niuiuei and assault are tried at the assizes now, arid how many were tried tr u years ago; wnai the value of landed propeily in the south ot Ireland is now, and what it was when orange viceioy presided at the castle." The liberal government is in the honourable position ot oeing able to court inquiry, troth as to tis past conduct and us luiuie poin t þÿ

It has no need of concealment þÿ it need not borrow Sir K. Reel's ail ol dixiemos misrepresentation. To aitack monopoly, to lighten the burden on the labouring classes, io oppose the imposition ot new taxes in þÿ a woiu io use the expressive and admirable language ol Lord John Russell at the city meeting, to protect the unprotected, huch is lire honest avowed, siraighltor ward policy ot the pit sent ministers By this they will stand or tall.

A EW AND EXTRAORDINARY IM- PLEMENT Ot WAR. House of Commons, Wednesday June 16. Mr Wakley said, in the month of August, in last year, an editorial notice appeared in the Times newspaper, stating that there was in the possession of a certain gentleman a discovery of enormous power, calculated to affect to an extraordinary degree all future warfare on the lace of the civilised globe, and an account was given of certain proceedings which took place before the late King Wil-

liam the Fourth and the lords of the admiral ty. Subsequently it was stated, investigations were made, and their results laid before Lord .Melbourne, and that noble lord himseif instituted an inquiry, and referred the matter to the lords of the admiralty. That notice in August was followed by three in September, and there the matter appeared to rest until February in the present year, when an account was given of an experiment which was made on a sheet of water in Essex, the property of a Mr. Royd. in the presence of Sir R. Reel, Sir George Murray, Sir H. Hardinge, Sir F. Burdett, Lord In vest re, Col. Vernon, Captain Webster, and others, who were utterly astonished at what they sawr. A boat, weighing as was stated two tons and a half, and containing live tons of solid timber, fastened together with iron screws and spikes of great length and power, was set in motion, and at a given signal was stopped, and was blown, according to the words of the reporter. into ten thousand fragments. There could have been no disguise or deception it was sta'ed, lor Captain Britten (who was not a friend of Mr Warner, the inventor) had superintended the proceedings, and Mr, Warner did not go near the object. He thought the house arid ihecountiy were entitled to information on a subject of such importance affecting the maritime power of the country, and a. so il regarded in an economical point ol view, as well as with reference to the interests ol humanity, lor il such a power

wag in i xistenc.o there would be an end to war. as tew persons would like to expose themselves to such a power, and therefore he wished to know from the noble lord, who was alleged to have witnessed the experiments, wlieiiier i he accounts which had been published of tin in were true.

Lord Ingestre said he very much regretted that ibis subject had been brought before the public eiiliei in a newspaper or pamphlet, or in that house, because he conceived ihat this immense power ought to be secured to this country with as much secrecy as possible þÿ He had been aware of this invention for upwatds of a year. His attention had been first diawn to it In an indistinct paragraph which he had seen by accident, and in which he thought there was more than met the eye, and from that moment to the preseni his conviction had been strengthened that ihe acquisition of such a power was ot the greatest possible moment to the country He had Ihe less hrsila. lion in stating this opinion, as it was confirmed bv tnose of many distinguished officers, and, amongst others, by Admiral King and Sir Thomas Hardinge. whose opinions on the subject had been stated to the government. He could refer also to an offirer of distinction whose authority would be allowed to be very high þÿ 8nr George Murray, who had, at his (Lord Ingesire's) solicitation, gone to witness the second experiment, and he w as, like every one else, struck with the immense power exhibited He had since had communications with the first lord of the treasury , and had requested that the matter mighl he inquired into, and obtained from ihe noble lord at ihe head of the treasury an acquiescence in that opinion The inventor had now been for ten years endeavouring to press upon the government the necessity of looking into the matter. He was

pressed in a way which he (Lord Ingestre) need not describe, and ihe country owed him the greatest possible gratitude for having resisted the most tempting offers from other countries, by which he could have relieved

himself from his embarrassments ; but his answer invariably had been, that he would sacrifice his personal interests, that the advanta ges of this discovery might be reserved for his own country. (Cheers.) This individual had had, through him (Lord Ingestre) communications with the first lord of the treasury, personally and by letter. He had not failed to urge upon that noble lord the necessity of ascertaining whether this discovery was worth having or not. That could be easily ascertained in a short time, and that was all he asked. It was a cruelty to the individual, and an injustice to the country, not to inquire into the subject. It had been his intention, after having urged the subject upon the first lord to the treasury as far as possible, to have brought the subject before the house, if the session had proceeded to its ordinary termination. He repeated his regret that the matter had been thus prematurely made public, because it would increase the difficulty of negotiations between the prime minister and the inventor. Sir F Burdett had seen the experiments and although he was no authority on the sub ject. nor could anv one who had not been in service duly appreciate the effect of this discovery, yet this he could say, that what he had seen was, in his mind, the most astonishing sight that could he conceived, and the in strument being so small and trifling compared with the effect produced it appeared quite a marvel. It was clear that some means of explosion more powerful than gunpowder had

been discovered. The hon hart, then proceeded to give description of the effects of a the explosion, which shattered large and solid pieces of oak fastened together in the strongest manner with iron clamps, shivered them from a distance of 200 01 300 yards, as if they had been struck by lightning, and carried some of the fragments over a large grove of high trees He hoped, as attention had now been called to the subject, that some means would be taken to secure to the country a power of such magnitude so far btyond anything that had ever been seen or heard of, and so infinitely beyond any means now used tor the same purposes, Mr. Brotherton protested against giving encouragement to those who employed their genius in discoveries injurious and destructive to mankind, instead of devoting it to the noble purpose of promoting peace and happiness among their fellow-creatures.

( From the Times.) Speak ! for thoa hast a voice, perpetual sea! TJft up ihy duijjes with some Fiscal word ohow where tiie pilgrims of the waters be, For whom a þÿnation thrilling s heart is þÿstill d.
Down to thy waves the\ went in joyous pride, They trod witti sreadtasl feet thy billowy way, The eves of wondering men beheld them glide Swift in the arrowy distance þÿ where are they ?
Didst thou in e up.m that mighty frame. Mad that the strength of man with thee should strive, Aad proud thy rival element to tame, Didst swaiiow them in conscious depths alive?
Or, shorn and powerless, hast thou bade them lie Their stately slop, a carcase of the foam ? Where still they watch the ocean and the shy, And fondly dre .in that they have yet a home !
Doth h >pe þÿs soothe ill their souls or gladness thrill? Is peace aond those wanderers of the foam ? Say. i the old affection yearning still With ail the blessed memories of home?
Or is it over ? Life and breath and thought, The living feature and the breathing form ; Is the strong man become a thing of nought, And the rich blood of rank no onger warm?
Thou antwerest not, thou stern and haughty sea, There is no sound in earth, or wave, or air. Roll on. ve tears ! Oh what can comfort be To hearts that past for hope, but breathe despair 5
Nay, mourner, there is sunlight on the deep, A gentle rainbow on the darkling cloud ; A voice more mighty than t he floods, will sweep The shore of tempests when the storm is loud !
What though they woke the whirlwinds of the west, Or roused the tempest from bis eastern lair, Or clave the cloud with thunder hi its þÿbreast, Lord of the awful waters, thou wert there !
All merciful! The fate þÿ the day þÿ were thine; Thou didst receive them from the seething sea ; Thy love too deep, Thy mercy too divine, To quench them in an hour unworthy Thee.

MONEY MUIKET. SATURDAY. That the value of the funded as well as of the landed property of the country depends most materially upon an adequate protection to both being maintained, is not denied by an\ party having practical knowledge upon such subjects. The public securities have since this day week been in some degree in juriouslv influenced by the apprehension that the crops have been affected by the continued prevalence of unseasonable weather. Should the harvest prove deficient, and an importation of foreign grain be rendered necessary there cannot be a doubt that the value of the funds must recede very materially. The agriculturists of the United Kingdom would a so have cause f r alarm, as the agitation of the corn repeal question would then he continued, the agitators not deeming it worth while to consider the privations and losses of the landowners at periods when there has been a succession of good crops, accompanied by very low prices, and when it will be recollected by those of our readers interested in such matters, a diminution of rents was submitted to bv most of the proprietors of the Soil on each audit day. Our national securities are rather firmer to day, but only a moderate business has been done. Consols for immediate transfer have r< ansed 89j> to |, and for the Account to 90 sellers.

THE þÿQUEEN S SPEECH. Already have parties commenced to speculate on the nature of the speech with which her Majesty will open the new Parliament þÿ Some expect that it will be peculiarly unintelligible and milk <fe water. Others hold a contrary opinion. One of the London papers now before us says þÿ þÿ Of one thing we feel confident, that whether actually present or not, her Majesty's Speech will hear the impress of her firm and vigorous spirit, and will show no traces of indecision or- regret. She has done her duty better by the people than the people have done their duty by her; and having endeavoured to lighten their burthens, she is not likely to express repentance for the attempt, although ill sustained by them. þÿ The þÿQueen speech s then, framed under the advice of her present Ministers, will be racy and uncompromising. They can give her no other counsel, without proclaiming themselves to be unworthy of her confiþÿdence rash in attack, and cravens in defeat ; and we hope that it is upon this ground tha the two parties will join issue."

From the New York European, August 4. china. India, and egypt. The last dates are þÿ from Macao the 2d of April. Calcutta the 5th of June, Bombay the IHth of June, and from Alexandria the 19th of July. Bombay, Junk þÿ19. Our accounts from China are to the 2d of April, only two days later than those brought by the steamer Queen on the 29th of that month, and which we received in June. Commodore Sir Gordon Bremer, who bad been in Calcutta since the middle of March, left that place for Canton in the steamer Queen on the 25th ol May, to resume his offices as naval commander and joint plenipotentiary in China. He takes with him numerous reinforcements, and others are following in transports. The whole fleet mav be expected to reach Canton bv the beginning of July. As soon as his excellency rejoins the squadron, there can be but little doubt that hostile operations will be renewed It is probable this expedition will be toolateto get up the Pei ho this year. þÿ hey I may retake Chusan, and the steamers might reconnoitre to the noth ward, but we doubt if matters will be finally arranged until the season of 1S42 The results of this supplementary expedition are looked forward to with the greatest anxiety, for upon the prudent management of the force must entirely depend the question of our future relations with the Chinese. At Macao our troops and the fleet still remained in position awaiting reinforcements ' and orders, while the Emperor of China, inflamed to the highest pitch of anger by the presumptuous proceedings ofthe British in at-

tacking his towns and destroying his ships, was issuing furious edicts and decrees against them. One of his edicts, in reference to the capture of the Bogue Forts, contains the following words: þÿ þÿ They have carried their unsubmissive rebellion to this extreme, and ! (the emperor) now swear that both powers shall not stand ; one or other must conquer or die.'

The 19th of the present month is the day on which the writs are returnable for the new parliament, hut the royal speech will not be delivered until the 24th. It is not settled whether the qneen will open the session in person, nor whether there is to be an opposition to the re-election of Mr. Shaw I.efevre as speaker. This would cost the public his pension of £4000 per annum, and Sir Robert Feel many naturally be unwilling to commence with such a dead weight. At the same time, it is considered not desirable for a conservative ministry to have a political opponent in the þÿspeaker c s hair, and very strong remonstrances are made by the metropolitan and provincial press against what they term an act of madness suicidal to their party. þÿ The speaker, it should be observed, has the nomination of the committees to try election petitions. We are sorry it is not in our power to announce any improvement either in the state or prospects of trade The accounts from the munufacturing districts are, if possible more gloomy than ever. Failures are frequent, and in the town of Paislv there have) been no fewer than thirteen, the aggregate of the engagements of the unfortunate parties being, it is said, not less than three hundred thousand pounds. Besides the shock which

this calamity must give to commercial credit, it will cause much distiess in the community of that district. We hear also that large concerns ill l.ancash're are about to be closed in consequence of declining trade.

From the London Observer, August 15. " LIVERPOOL, Saturday Morning. "Cunnrd's fine steamer Caledonia arrived here this morning, after an excellent passage from Halifax of ten days. She brings Halifax papers of the 3d. Boston of the 1st, and New York of July 31. " The most gratifying feature in the papers is the intelligence they convey respecting the crops, which are every where promising and abundant. The crops of cotton and corn never, it is said, looked better. In many of the States the corn had been harvested in the finest condition In the present gloomy prospect of the harvest in England, this intelligence is doubly welcome, but, unhappily, our sliding scale would render an importation of American flour or corn two or three months hence, a matter of mere speculation. " The atiair of M'Leod continues to be discussed in the papers and referred to in Congress, in a somewhat better tone and spirit than by the previous arrival. His trial is fixed to take place at Utica, in the State of New York, in September."

A very large contract is announced hv the commissioners for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the Navy. It is for not less than 15,000 navy tierces of beef, and 10,000 tierces of pork. The last contract was much below these quantities, and it shows that it is the intention of Government to maintain in the most efficient state the naval department of the kingdom. While doubt exists on the adjustment of the Boundary question, it is probably the desire of the Ministers to show to the American Executive that, "if the worst come to the worst," the " tight little island" is prepared to vindicate her right to the disputed land.

Parker arrived at Aden on their way to China early on the morning of die 29th of June, and proceeded to Bombay on the afternoon of the same day. Sir Henry Pottinger purposed set off for China in one of the to Company's steam frigates as soon as practicable alter reaching Bombay, arid expected to rcaeli China the first week in August. Sir Henry's health appeared perfectly re established by bis trip, and be embarked from Aden in the full enjoy ment of all his mental and bodily eneigies. Sir \V Parker was much disappointed on finding that the Eridymion frigate had left Aden for Bombay, as it was the admiral's wish to have hoisted his flag on board her. I be Endvmion reached Aden in a leaky state, having struck on a reef in the Mozambique Channel ; and (.'up tain Grev deemed it requisite to sail for Bornbay, that the frigate might fie decked and ex atnined. On her voyage out she sprung her mainmast between decks, and ibis, with a leak which could not he got at, determined

Captain Grev not to await ihe arrival of Sir VV Paik cr. The Admiral will probably proceed in her to China from Bombay. We have good authority for stating tiiat Sir H. Poitinger lias proceeded to China with the most ample powers, and that his policy has not been restricted by minute instructions þÿ li is probable that on his arrival in China he will demand, by an ultimatum, the terms on which peace can he concluded ; and if not immediately acceded to he will direct our combined iand and sea forces against Pekin. We have great confidence in the firm and unflinching character of Sir Henry Pottinger, and we sincerely believe that a more fir person could not have been selecied to carry out the energetic measures now required.

PARLIAMENTARY MEASURES ON THE MEETING OF THE TWO HOUSES. In a course of conduct, towards the accomplishment of any great end, which requires uniformity of councils, and a steady applioa" tion and direction of them towards the accomplishment of the main object, there is nothing which is attended with more practical mischief. and- which brings more perplexity upon those who have to take the lead in such councils, than the necessity ol turning out of the way so as to escape collateral difficulties. At the very ouiset of the conservative minis try, Air R. Peel has unfortunately fallen into this embarrassment. 1 he detern ination as to the re-election of the Speaker has not given general satisfaction even to his own party, and already has produced an inconvenient impression upon the public mind. It is deemed by many to be a mark of weakness on the part of the conservative leader, and the observation frequenily occurs in public assemblies, that he would not have made this concession except under the feeling thai he did not possess that authority over his own party which is so essentially necessary for a political leader. N >w, it is impossible to look at the returns in the general election, without being diiven to the conclusion, that the parliament w ill scarcely assemble, before innumerable petilions will be brougtit up. both against many of ihe borough returns m England, and nearly aii tiie radical counties in lieland Is it not obvious, thai all this requires a vigorous and impartial Speaker, and one who will exercise his function of appointing chairmen with-

out fear or favour ; in which words it is not our purpose to include any uncivil insinuation against the honor and integrity of Mr. Ahaw Lefevre ; we speak only of that bias, which a particular state of feeling will insensibly exercise over the strongest mind and the most unsullied personal honour. There is not, for example, a more unsuspected class of men than the whole bench of English judges ; hut who would choose to commit the decision o' his case to any one of them who might happen to have a diiect and personal interest in the issue ? But the choice is now concluded, and there is an end of it. We have only slated, as public writeis, the general feeling upon the subject, and dismissing all further bickering upon a by-gone cause ol dissension and disagreement, we now cheerfully turn to the ironside-

fation of those public measures whieh will, probably, follow the formation of a new ministry . In our foreign policy, there are several subjects ot much dilliculiy. ami amontrst them the present proceedings of the American government towards Mr Al'l.eod. it is manifest that his life is in danger, and his long imprisonment is also a personal hardship and injust ee, which renders it incurnhent upon the honour and character of ihe English government to interfere effectually, and without any delay. The cuuntry ought to know w hat instructions were given to our minister, Mr. Fox, and what Lord Palmers ton direcied our ambassador to do when appiised of the intention of the American government to put JM'Leod 011 his trial We have claimed him, we are told.thiogh the authority of the minister at Washington ; þÿ we ought to be informed what answer was returned to that claim, and how and why it was eluded. All these questions should be put and answered, and though we ought never to forget the dreadful consequences ol a national war to both countries, so far as regards human happiness and suflering. it also becomes us to protect the life and liberty of our own subject.

Marriage op the Princess Clementine. þÿ It is said that apprehensions are entertained of the Papal Court raising objections to the marriage of the Hereditary Prince of Saxe Coburg with the Princess Clementine, on account of the difference of religion, the þÿl ope having already complained of the young Prince of \V urtemburg, son of the Princess Marie, not being brought up a catholic, as his mother had promised Besides this difficulty, it is said there are some family matters to settle, and it is on this account that the reigning Duke of Saxe Coburg is going to hold a congres de famille at Gotha, at which the Duchess ol Kent, the Prince of Leiningen, and the other members of the house will be present. Baron Maltravers, the title bv w'hich the Earl of Surrey has been called to the Upper House, was a creation in the reign of Henry HI., and came into the Howard family by the marriage of Sir John Fitzalan, called Arundel, with Eleanor, daughter of the fourth baron. Death of Madame Catalani þÿ By letters received in town yesterday we are sorry to learn that this distinguished singer expired at her Casino, on the banks of Laco di Como, on Sunday the 20lh ult., in the Gist year of her age. The Ei 'Piirates Expedition. þÿ Letters from Aleppo mention that the Euphrates expedition had been crowned with success þÿ 1 wosteam-boats had reached Beles in safety.

The Colonial Bank Shares have remained at 9' pm. The half yearly meeting of the proprietors of this bank was held yesterday, when a most favourable report was read of the proceedings of the corporation in the West Indies, where the operations of the bank are principally carried on. At the recommendation ol the court of directors a dividend of 4 per cent, for the half year was declared upon the paid-up capital of the bank, which amounts to half a million of sterling.

The substance ol the privileges petitioned for by the Company, a copy of which accompanies the message, may be enumerated as follows : þÿ That the þÿCompany v s essels be considered in every respect as English ships of war. That they be exempt from tonnage, and all port dues, Ate. lhat the coal imported by the Company for its use, be free of duty, and the vessels importing it. tree of tonnage and port dues. 1 bat the þÿCompany v s essels be allowed to land or embark passengers, specie, luggage, and parcels, at all hours of the day or night, subject to the regulations of the customaiy authorities. I hat the þÿCompany s vessels be also permitted to land any packages of merchandize they may have on freight, at all hours of the day or night, previous notice thereof being

given to the Customs, and without suffering thereby either in their privileges or exemptions ; the Company guaranteeing that no package of such description shall he landed without the corresponding permit of the Customs. country by the establishment of tlieir ves- " The Company likewise hope the Government will construct a light house at Chagres, for the guidance and safety of their vessels arriving at night.

Conservative Prospects. þÿ In our last paper we threw a hasty glanee over this subjeet as regarded the counties, and showed that the conservative gain in the counties alone would be fourteen seats; to these we have now to add, that Roxburghshire is abandoned by the whigs, and Mr Scott, the conservative, will become its representative. þÿ In Rutlandshire, we have also to announce that Mr Dawnev steps forward to oppose Noel and Heathcote ; here will he an un doubted gain ; whilst in the neighbouring ' hood went out to meet her, and escorted her countv of Lincoln, Mr. Cust. a son of Lord Brownlow, has started to oppose Lord Tforsley. A letter addressed to the Comptroller of these Customs by a Custom House Cutter received this morning, gives the following particulars of the capture of a piratical schooner. Balize, 1st June. After having taken possession, at -Semphire Key, of the sloop mentioned in my letter dated from Passe Christian, 1 embarked on board the IT' S. steamer Izard, taking said sloop in tow, bound to Old harbour Key. where I anchored on the 20th May. Here I learned from a fisherman, that on the North point of Chandelier island, 1 would find a vessel, either pirate or contrabandist. 1 hastened to put a couple of hands on board the sloop to navigate her, and proceeded in the Izard to the spot pointed out ; in fact, 1 saw at an anchor there, a small schooner painted black, which I instantly searched » but with the exception of a quantity of large oars, 1 fell in with nothing in her calculated to justify the suspicion of the fisherman. þÿ The Captain not being on board, 1 was informed hv a man named Gllisahbot, who was there with six more of the crew, that their object was to spend the whole summer in that quarter, fishing, having a due license to that effect l returned to the steamer, and anchored at a mile distant from the schooner ; my doubts regarding her character not being altogether removed, 1 started again the next morning, with a fresh breeze from the N. W. ; and on first nearing her, descried a man throw himself overboard, swimming towards me and calling aloud for protection. 1 tacked ship

forthwith and secured the man at the very moment he vva3 about being overtaken by a skirt sent after him ; on coming on board the steamer, he stated his name to be Thompson, and that he was taken by force in Mobile, that he had no doubt of the schooner being a pirate as a proof ol which he proposed to shew me the places, where there were arms concealed with this information, I came to ; an anchor alongside of her, and led on by this man f discovered arms, powder and shots, in abundance ; satisfied then of the truth, and finding the conclusion of Mr. Wadsworth, member of the Legislature and of JJr. Harrison, who accompanied me, to coincide with my own, I seized the vessel, and after ransferrtng all the arms and ammunitions on board the Izard, I look her in tow and hastened on here, where I arrived with my prize and had tiie seven prisoners set in chains pro-

From the New York Commercial Advertiser, June 24, 1841. Tub Supposed Piracy þÿ Knowing what we do know, at this present time of writing, there is some thing irresistibly ludicrous in the paragtaphs with which the New Orleans papers teem, concerning the þÿ horrible catas þÿtrophe of the ship Charles. That the passengers were all robbed and murdered is assumed as unquestionable ; and hosts of additional deveiopeinents, each more fearful than its predecessor, are daily brought to light, to the infinite horror of the editors and their excitable readers. For example here is one, furnished by the Picayune of the 1 3th. ID We are informed by Capt Butler that he found, in ths steerage- hatch of the ship Charles yesterday, some fearful evidences of crime wnich had not been before discovered. Among the rubbish which had been thmst aside unnoticed was the dress of a female apparently new, and a very good black coat There was also the upper portion of a þÿfemale s dress, which bears the appearance of having been violently torn from the wearer ; the skirt entirely missing ; the inside part of the right breast of tins fragment is dappled with blood, and there is likewise some blood upon the left breast; there is a small incision, which seems to have been made by a dirk or dagger The garment is of gingham, white with blue stripe?. Under all the circumstances there appears he something in this mute witness to which indicates a tale of horror yet to be told We are not disposed to give currency to the thousand and one idle stones which are daily circulated, but ail properly attested

evidence, tending to throw any light upon this melancholy affair, should be laid before the public. We are assured on the beat of authority that the dog, found in the boat, belonging to the captain of the Charles, now passes d great portion of his time ou that vessel, in the place on deck where the greatest quantity ol blood was first discovered, demon

stiating the most unequivocal and touching distress and sorrow. Those who understand the unerring ir.siinct and faithfulness of these animals know how much importance ought to be attached to tins extraordinary occuirence. Then the valiant threatenings and promises of the parties engaged in the laudable search, lor the supposed pirates, although quite natural and, if the affair was yet wrapped in mystery, n either extravagant nor laughable, do seem especially ridiculous, now that the mystery is explained We cannot suppress a smile at them, even while recognizing the zeal and energy which the supposed occasion has called forth. There is a good lesson for us all, however, in the res ill of this much lalkeu of matter. It is, to he cautious in believing all ihe reports that come before us, prejudicial to the good name ol individuals, and tn dtawing unfavotable conclusions from even the most unaccountable appearances As in the present case, a very simple explanation may often he given to facts that without it bear a startling J aspect. f>OOo þÿ LATEST FROM ENGLAND.

The Harvest. þÿ The improvement in the crops from the rains is something quite wonderful We never remember so important a benefit. The wheats are increased in the ear immensely, and the growth of the barley both in the stalk and ear is astonishing. An agricultur st, upon whom we can rely, assures ns that his barleys have risen 12 inches in 10 days. But we nevertheless apprehend that neither crop will be equal to that of last year though there are prodigiously fine appearances on some of the heavy and light lands of Norfolk. The second crop of hay will be greatlv increased. We have only to hope for a fortnight of sunshine to bring on an early harvest, þÿ JSorwich Met cury.

While the community of Jamaica had been supposing that Cuba, one of the strong hob's of slavery, had hitherto remained alnu, . t alone, uninfluenced by Antislavery doctrines or Anti slavery exertions, we find not oi ly that an attempt to cultivate sugar and coffee by free labor in that island has been made, but that a memorial has been presented to the Executive by proprietors of estates, in favor of the abolition of slavery, and that the Governor has expressed his friendship to the measure, having, as a first step, refused the bounty on the admission of slaves invariably presented to his predecessors, and declared his intention of not clearing out vessels bound fur the coast of Africa. This is gratifying intelligence, and such as will gladden the hearts of the Anti slavery party. Cuba, the strong hold of the enemy has been shaken her people have began to capitulate, they know that þÿ the slave trade is the sole and exclusive cause of the displeasure with which the increasing agricultural and commercial prosperity of the island is regarded by all powerful England, and that the trade is the real or apparent motive for its having become the target lor her diplomatic hostility, and knowing this they fear. Must not þÿ emancipation speedily be the result, þÿ Barbadian August 4.

Little did we think- yesterday, in penning a brief paragraph in commendation of the Erie, that, to-day, we should be called upon to record the destruction of that boat, together with n loss of life unequalled on our own, or almost any other waters. The Erie left the dock at 10 minutes past 4 P M .. loaded with merchandize destined for Chicago, and, as nearly as now can be ascertained, about two hundred persons, including passengers and crew on board. The boat had been thoroughly overhauled, and although the wind was blowing fresh, every thing promised a pleasant and prosperous voyage. Nothing occurred to mar this prospect till about 8, wh"n the boat was oft Silver Creek, about 8 miles from shore, and 33 miles from the city, when a slight explosion was heard, and immediately, instantaneously almost, the whole vessel was enveloped in flame. C'npt. Titus, who was on the upper deck at the time, rushed to the ladies' cabin to obtain the life preservers, of which there were from 90 to 100 on board ; but so rapid had been the progress ol the flames; he found it impossible to enter the cabin. He returned to the upper deck, on his way giving orders to the engineer to stop the engine, the wind and the head way of the boat increasing the fierceness of the flames and driving them att. The engineer replied that in consequence ol the

flames he could not reach the engine. The stearman was instantly directed to put the helm hard a starboard The vessel swung glowlv round, heading to the shore, and the bo. its þÿ there were three on board w< re then ordered to be lowered. Two of the boats were lowered, but in consequence ol she heavy sea on, and the headway ot the vessel, they both swamped as soon as they touched wafer We will not attempt to describe the awful and appalling condition of the passengers Some were frantic with fear and horror, others plunged headlong madly into the water, others again seized upon any thing buoyant uuon which thev could lay hands þÿ The small boat forward had been lowered þÿ It was alongside t he wheel, with three or four peisons in it, when the captain jumped in and the boat immediately dropped astern and filled with water. A lady floated by with a life preserver on She cried for help. There was no safety in the boat. The captain threw her the only oar in the boat. She caught the oar and was saved. It was Mrs l.vnde, of Milwaukie. and she was the only lady saved. The Clinton left here in the morning, but in consequence of the wind had put into Dunkirk She lay there till nearly sunset, at which time she ran out, and had proceeded as far as Barcelona, when just at
